newsitem.title: USA: Volatile CBOT July soybeans prompts basis switch.
newsitem.headline: Volatile CBOT July soybeans prompts basis switch.

text.p: Some U.S. Midwest grain buyers this week switched cash soybean basis bids to the Chicago Board of Trade August or November soybean contracts from the CBOT July, a move analysts said reflects the industry's concern about the potential volatility in the July contract.

"I think everyone is afraid of being short the July," said Charlie Sernatinger, vice president of Chicago grain sales for E.D.& F Man International. "They probably have an innate bias that the July will continue to gain on the other months."

The basis switch occurred earlier than normal this year because of the potential for sharp price gains in the CBOT July, analysts and grain dealers said. Sharp price gains could make it costly for grain firms should they have to liquidate short hedge positions.
"Basically, we are trying to avoid the volatility in the July option," said an Indiana soybean dealer.

Deliverable soybean supplies are low and farmers are selling only small amounts of the few soybeans they have, a combination that has made for volatile action in CBOT July futures. Further erratic price moves are anticipated.
On May 29, CBOT July soybeans sped to limit gains on news deliverable supplies in Chicago plummeted to 35,000 bushels after a grain firm pulled 1.245 million bushels out of deliverable position.
Analysts said CBOT July soybeans could challenge the contract high of $9.02 per bushel. Tuesday morning CBOT July soybeans reached a high of $8.75.
Soybean dealers said switching cash bids to CBOT August and November also aids soybean crushers in setting profitable but competitive prices for their soymeal and soyoil.

One Ohio grain firm bid 185 cents per bushel over the CBOT November soybeans Wednesday versus its six cents over the July bid Tuesday. In Cedar Rapids, Iowa, another firm's bid went to 170 cents over November from July price Tuesday. Based on Monday's close, the changes reflect price decreases of 4.25 to 13.25 cents, respectively.
Analysts said the lowering of cash bids may have been done to scare farmers into selling before bids fall further, a tactic analysts believe will fail.
Farmers who still own soybeans from last year probably will resist selling until they are confident of a decent crop this year, analysts said.

"They are not going to be scared out right now," said Doug Hjort, president of Hjort Associates, a Des Moines-based grain brokerage firm. "I don't imagine they will sell more until they are assured of a crop."
